newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lack of funds threaten Russia's space programme.
newsitem.headline: Lack of funds threaten Russia's space programme.

text.p: Russia may have to abandon its manned space programme next year due to a severe shortage of funds, a senior space official said on Thursday.
Yuri Koptev, general director of the Russian space agency, told a gathering of government ministers that Russia also has "practically no reserve of rockets".
"We will need two or three years of stable and adequate financing to restore stocks of booster rockets," Koptev said in comments reported by Russian news agencies.
He said that about 50 percent of orbiting Russian communication satellites may cease to exist "at any time" because they are outdated.

But Yuri Poletayev, chief of the space launch department at the commercial space organisation Glavkosmos, told Reuters that Russia would not allow its Mir space station, in orbit for 10 years, to stop working.
"Mir deals with Russia's only manned space programme," Poletayev said. "It is our national pride and ... a source of funds from the West."
The Russian space agency receives money for Western cosmonauts based on the Mir station.

However Poletayev said that Russian rocket-makers were in deep crisis. "About 80 percent of engineers and workers have left the space industry," he said. "Russia has already lost many space professionals".
"Young people do not want to study space subjects at university or technical institute because they are no longer presitigious," Poletayev added.
Russia's commercial space organisations face serious problems because they depend on the rocket-makers, he said.
"These organisations that work under contract with Western partners will not survive if the government does not help Russia's space industry," he said.
A cash shortage has thrown into jeopardy Russia's participation in the creation of the Alpha space orbiting station, due to replace Mir in the next century.

Koptev said lack of money meant the Alpha "service module" would not be ready as scheduled. But last week the module's maker -- Khrunichev space centre -- said that it planned to complete production next July, using its own funds and loans.
Last month Khrunichev finished building the first Alpha module under a $190 million contract with U.S. Boeing Co. It will be sent into orbit in 1997.
The United States, the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan are also involved in the Alpha project, which aims to complete the space station early in the next century.
